transcript.text: Alright, let's get this architecture review underway. We need to decide on the approach for our centralized audit-log pipeline for administrative actions. Before I record any final design, I want to hear from compliance and data platform on their constraints. Could someone from compliance start by walking us through the requirements — things like ordering guarantees, retention, immutability, and any tamper-evidence needs? And then data platform, please share your constraints around throughput, consumer patterns, and storage. That way we can properly evaluate the three options on the table: direct Kafka publishing, a managed cloud queue, and the transactional-outbox-to-Kafka design.

Theo, I appreciate you previewing that you have throughput and emission-constraint findings; please hold as you said until compliance has fully walked through all their requirements. transcript.text: Thanks, Riley. Yes, there are several additional compliance constraints we need to capture. First, on ordering: audit records for administrative actions must preserve causal ordering within a given service — we cannot have an admin action's audit record arrive out of order relative to related events from the same service, as that would undermine the integrity of an audit trail. Second, on tamper-evidence: the pipeline must provide cryptographic tamper-evidence — we need to be able to demonstrate that a record has not been altered between emission and long-term storage. This likely means some form of chaining or hashing of consecutive records, or append-only storage with integrity verification. Third, on access logging: access to the audit records themselves must be logged — who read or queried audit data, when, and for what purpose. Fourth, on regulatory audit-access: we must support on-demand retrieval of records by authorized external auditors within a defined timeframe, which means the storage layer needs queryable indexing, not just raw append-only blobs. And finally, the immutability requirement I mentioned earlier means not just retention for 7 years, but a guarantee that no party — including privileged admins — can modify or delete records before the retention period expires. That combination of constraints is the complete compliance picture from my side. Theo, I'll hand it to you for the data platform constraints.

transcript.text: I have two key data platform findings to share. First, during an integration test for another service yesterday, I confirmed that the billing service can emit audit events reliably only through its transactional outbox into Kafka — direct publishing or a managed cloud queue won't work for that service. Second, my capacity review shows the pipeline must be configured with exactly 12 Kafka partitions to handle expected peak throughput. I haven't updated the design document with either of these findings yet.
transcript.speaker: A3

transcript.text: Thanks, Theo. Both findings are significant. The billing service constraint — that it can only emit reliably through a transactional outbox into Kafka — effectively eliminates direct Kafka publishing and the managed cloud queue as options for that service, which means the transactional-outbox-to-Kafka design is the only architecture that can accommodate all services. And the 12-partition requirement for peak throughput is noted as a hard configuration parameter. Before I record the final design, let me make sure I'm synthesizing everything correctly. Mina, from compliance: 7-year immutable retention with customer-managed encryption, causal ordering per service, cryptographic tamper-evidence via chaining or hashing, access logging on the audit data itself, and queryable indexing for external auditor retrieval. Theo, from data platform: billing service requires transactional-outbox-to-Kafka, and exactly 12 Kafka partitions for peak throughput. Given that the billing service constraint forces the transactional-outbox-to-Kafka approach, and that approach also satisfies the ordering and reliability requirements from compliance, I'm prepared to settle on the transactional-outbox-to-Kafka design as our production architecture. Are there any objections or anything else either of you need on the record before I record the final design and follow-up commitments?
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: No objections from compliance, Riley. The transactional-outbox-to-Kafka design can satisfy all the compliance constraints I laid out, provided we capture the following as follow-up commitments in the design record: (1) the long-term storage layer must enforce immutable 7-year retention with customer-managed key encryption and no privileged deletion path; (2) the outbox-to-Kafka flow must preserve causal ordering per service — I'd want to confirm that the 12-partition configuration and the partitioning strategy maintain that guarantee, since ordering is only preserved within a single partition; (3) cryptographic tamper-evidence via chaining or hashing must be applied before or at long-term storage write; (4) access logging on the audit data itself must be implemented; and (5) the storage layer must support queryable indexing for external auditor retrieval within the defined timeframe. I'd like one explicit commitment from the data platform side on how partitioning will be keyed to preserve per-service causal ordering before this is finalized.

transcript.text: Good question from Mina on partitioning strategy, and I want to give a concrete commitment here. To preserve per-service causal ordering, we should key the Kafka partition by service ID — that way all audit events from a given service, including the billing service, land on the same partition and maintain their causal order. With exactly 12 partitions, we'll have sufficient parallelism for peak throughput while preserving the per-service ordering guarantee compliance requires. I want to flag one thing for the record though: Mina's point about ordering being preserved only within a single partition is correct, and it means our partitioning key must be the service ID — not a composite key that could split a service's events across partitions. That's a hard design commitment from my side. As for the other follow-up commitments, I can commit to: configuring the long-term storage layer with the immutable 7-year retention and customer-managed key encryption as specified by compliance; and ensuring the consumer side of the pipeline supports the queryable indexing and access logging requirements. The tamper-evidence via chaining or hashing is something I'd want to collaborate with compliance on — specifically whether it should be applied at the outbox emission point or at the long-term storage write, since that affects where we compute and store the chain hashes. Riley, before you record the final design, I'd like to note that I still need to update the design document with both the billing service outbox constraint and the 12-partition requirement — that should be captured as a follow-up commitment as well.

commitments.detail: Configure long-term storage layer with immutable 7-year retention, customer-managed key encryption, and no privileged deletion path.
Key Kafka partitions by service ID only — not a composite key — to preserve per-service causal ordering within a single partition. Exactly 12 partitions.
Collaborate on where to apply cryptographic tamper-evidence (chaining or hashing) — at outbox emission point or at long-term storage write — and implement accordingly.
Implement access logging on the audit data itself — who read or queried audit data, when, and for what purpose.
Ensure storage layer supports queryable indexing for on-demand external auditor retrieval within the defined timeframe.
Update the design document with both the billing service transactional-outbox constraint and the 12-partition requirement.
